Three lions die in Tokyo zoo as heatwave scorches East Asia
A record-breaking heatwave stretching across East Asia is straining animals, health systems and people.
Save
Share
By AFP and Reuters
Published On 4 Aug 20264 Aug 2026
Three lions at a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke, as record-breaking temperatures in East Asia have prompted South Korea’s president to declare a national disaster.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung told officials at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday to ensure support for those worst affected by the heat and inspect power systems as air conditioning demand surges.
The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency said the death toll from the heatwave has risen to 19, including 13 people aged 80 or above. Since May 15, at least 2,025 people have suffered heat-related illnesses nationwide.
“An even greater concern is that abnormal weather conditions make it highly likely that extreme weather will continue for a considerable period,” said Lee, who wants a major redesign of the disaster response system to cope with the hazardous conditions.
South Korea’s heat record has been broken three times over the past week, with the latest set at 42.5 degrees Celsius (108.5 degrees Fahrenheit) in the city of Yangsan on Sunday, the highest measured in 122 years of weather observations, according to the Korea Meteorological Administration.
The heat is not confined to South Korea. Across the border in North Korea, state media said heat advisories covering much of the country would stay in place through the week, as water parks in Pyongyang drew large crowds. Because North Korea does not have media freedom, the casualties there from the heatwave are unknown.
Record heat across East Asia
In Japan, nearly 18,600 people were taken to hospital for heatstroke between July 20 and 26, with 45 of them pronounced dead on arrival, according to the country’s fire and disaster management agency. Parts of the country have hit 40C in recent weeks, qualifying for the new designation “cruelly hot day”.
Advertisement
At Tama Zoological Park, Tokyo’s largest zoo, a three-year-old female lion called Mugi died last Tuesday, another called Ichigo died on Friday aged 11, and a third lioness called Luena died on Sunday aged 15.
“According to our veterinarian, the cause of the deaths is suspected to be heatstroke,” a zoo spokeswoman said.
“Even though lions are thought to be resistant to heat, zookeepers have been strengthening countermeasures to cope with Japan’s summer heat in recent years. Heat here comes with high humidity that is different from heat with dry air in Africa.”
Scientists say climate change driven by human activity is making heatwaves and other extreme weather events more frequent, longer-lasting and more intense.
In Europe, extreme heat and strong winds are causing wildfires and forcing evacuations in Greece, with Spain and France also on high alert for new blazes. Extreme heat was also recorded in the United States, increasing wildfire risks.
The United Nations weather agency warned on Friday that a strong El Nino is expected to intensify, starting this month. It warned that the phenomenon is likely to increase above-normal temperatures globally and significantly shift rainfall patterns.
El Nino is a naturally occurring periodic climate pattern in which warmer-than-usual waters in the Pacific Ocean disrupt global weather systems, typically intensifying heatwaves, droughts and storms in different parts of the world.

Italy's fourth heatwave this summer prompts emergency response-Xinhua
Italy's fourth heatwave this summer prompts emergency response
Source: Xinhua
Editor: huaxia
2026-08-05 01:17:15
Italy is battling its fourth major heatwave of the summer, with temperatures climbing above 40 degrees Celsius in parts of the country. Authorities are stepping up emergency measures amid mounting health, wildfire and agricultural concerns.
ROME, Aug. 4 (Xinhua) -- Italy is battling its fourth major heatwave of the summer, with temperatures climbing above 40 degrees Celsius in parts of the country, and a record number of cities placed under the highest heat alert. Authorities are stepping up emergency measures amid mounting health, wildfire and agricultural concerns.
The latest heatwave reached its peak on Monday, when the Health Ministry placed 25 of the country's 27 monitored cities under "red alert," the highest warning level possible issued for extreme heat.
The alert covered major cities including Rome, Milan, Florence, Bologna, Venice, Naples and Palermo, indicating weather conditions that pose health risks not only to vulnerable groups but also to healthy people exposed to prolonged high temperatures. Temperatures exceeded 40 degrees Celsius in several inland areas, with forecasters warning that relief is unlikely before the end of the week.
Health authorities have urged residents and tourists to avoid outdoor activities during the hottest hours of the day, stay hydrated and regularly check on elderly relatives and neighbors. The ministry has continued issuing daily heat bulletins covering 27 major cities, while coordinating emergency response efforts with regional governments and the Civil Protection Department under the national heat emergency plan.
The prolonged spell of hot, dry weather has also heightened the risk of wildfires, particularly across southern Italy and the country's two largest islands, Sicily and Sardinia. Firefighters remain on high alert as strong winds and exceptionally dry vegetation create favorable conditions for fast-moving blazes, while local authorities continue monitoring the areas considered most vulnerable.
Beyond public safety, the heatwave is placing increasing pressure on Italy's agricultural sector. Farmers have warned that persistent drought and extreme temperatures are reducing crop yields, increasing irrigation demand and exposing livestock to severe heat stress. In the northwestern Piedmont region, unusually high temperatures have accelerated grape ripening, prompting one of the earliest harvests in recent years.
The heatwave has also deepened drought conditions across the Po River basin, Italy's most important agricultural region. The Po River Basin Authority said persistently high temperatures and a lack of rainfall have left much of the basin under stress, with low river flows disrupting irrigation and raising concerns over drinking water supplies in several northern municipalities.
Authorities warned that saltwater intrusion in the Po Delta is threatening farmland, while tanker trucks have been deployed to deliver drinking water to some communities in the Lombardy region.
Lorenzo Giovannini, an atmospheric physicist at the University of Trento, told Italy's ANSA news agency that although it is difficult to predict exactly when each heatwave will occur, climate change is making such events "longer and more intense."
Persistently high temperatures, prolonged drought and declining water availability are increasingly becoming interconnected features of Italian summers, Giovannini explained, placing growing pressure on ecosystems, agriculture and public health. ■

At least 16 people have died in South Korea, as a record heatwave hits the country. President Lee Jae Myung has called for increased support for those affected amid warnings that extreme weather was becoming more frequent.
Between May 15 and August 2 this year, a total of 2,025 people have suffered heat-related illnesses, the interior ministry said in a statement.
What did President Lee say?
"We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, since this extreme weather is becoming normal," President Lee said at a cabinet meeting, where he urged officials to accelerate measures to protect the daily lives of people. He also called for inspections of power systems as demand for air conditioning rises.
South Korea's southeastern island city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5 degrees Celsius (108.5 degrees Fahrenheit) on Sunday, the highest measured in 122 years of observations, the national weather agency said.
After authorities issued their first-ever heatwave warning for parts of Seoul and Gyeonggi on Monday, the Korea Meteorological Administration extended it to the entire capital city on Tuesday. This was the first such advisory since the designation was introduced this year to alert the public about extreme temperatures.
South Korea grapples with historic heat wave
Temperatures in the capital hit 38 degrees Celsius at midday and were expected to fall only to about 29 degrees overnight. Residents were urged to stay indoors and drink plenty of water. The city has also designated about 4,000 public facilities as cooling centers.
While Seoul has a population of 9.6 million people, the wider metropolitan area is home to more than 25 million residents, which is about half of the country's population.
Europe wildfires continue as new heatwaves hit France, Spain
In Japan, cities have experienced "cruelly hot days" this summer, a new meteorological term the country uses to designate days with intense heat above 40 degrees. Tama Zoo in Tokyo announced Tuesday that three lions have died in the past week due to suspected complications from heatstroke as Japan swelters.
Europe has also faced a sweltering summer, with Germany's heat-related death toll for 2026 already surpassing every full-year total since 2016 — and expected to climb as another spell of extreme temperatures takes hold.

Thunderstorm and flash flood warning as latest heatwave comes to an end
Flash flooding could hit in areas with ground scorched by the recent heatwaves
Bookmark
Bookmark popover
Removed from bookmarks
Heavy rain could hit parts of the UK today during the final day of the latest sweltering heatwave.
There are thunderstorm warning in place for Northern Ireland from 12pm until 9pm today with warning of flooding and damage. Up to 30mm of rain could fall in an hour and there is also chance of hail.
Areas that do see a heavy downpour are at risk of flash flooding as scorched ground could cause significant water runoff.
It follows the driest July in England and Wales since records began. Parts of southern England may still not see a drop of rain, forecasters added.
Another record tumbled on Monday when the temperature reached 33.5C in Wisley in Surrey, marking the 20th day of 2026 when 32C or higher was recorded in the UK, exceeding the previous record of 19 days set in 1995, the Met Office said.
In the latest heat spike, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has amber heat health alerts in place for the East Midlands, East of England, South East and London until Wednesday morning.
There are also yellow heat health alerts for the North West, South West, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and The Humber, as the agency warns the latest high temperatures could put extra pressure on the NHS, with more vulnerable people likely to require medical treatment.
Outbreaks of rain and showers are forecast on Tuesday in Northern Ireland, Scotland, western England and Wales – but the Met Office has forecast a dry day for much of the Midlands, the east and south-east of England with warm sunshine and high humidity.
Temperatures are expected to decrease gradually in the second half of the week, and there is some more unsettled weather forecast for parts of the UK including a yellow warning for thunderstorms in Northern Ireland.
But the South East will continue to see little in the way of desperately needed rain, the Met Office has warned.
July was southern England’s driest month ever recorded, with the whole of Wales and half of England plunged into drought.
Farming leaders have warned it is “one of the most severe droughts many farmers and growers have lived through”, with poor yields, struggles to access water for fruit and vegetables and livestock keepers using winter feed for their animals.
The National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has demanded urgent action to secure water supplies for homegrown food production.
In July, 19 counties across England recorded effectively no rainfall – 1mm or less – across the whole of the month, the Met Office figures show.
The summer of extreme weather has seen two record-breaking heatwaves, in May and June, that led to more than 2,800 excess deaths, and two more heatwaves in July which have fuelled drought and wildfires.
Firefighters remained at the scene of a heathland blaze in Dunwich, Suffolk, on Monday, and crews declared a major incident as they tackled a huge wildfire in the Rhondda valley in South Wales.
Drone footage showed blackened ground and smoke billowing metres into the air over the valley, where South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) said the fire had affected 150 hectares of land, including forest, scrubland and vegetation.
What next?
The Met Office long range forecast says August will see a period of changeable weather, with initial forecasts predicting a mix of rain and showers alongside welcome drier interludes, particularly across the south.
As mid-August approaches, a significant shift in atmospheric pressure is anticipated. High pressure is expected to become more dominant across the north and northwest of the UK, while lower pressure systems may settle over southern and eastern regions. This pattern suggests an increased likelihood of frontal systems or thundery conditions affecting southern and eastern areas – a notable change compared to recent weeks. However, rainfall amounts are predicted to be quite variable, with some locations potentially experiencing relatively little precipitation.
Despite the unsettled outlook, temperatures are largely expected to remain above average, especially in the south, though without the exceptional heat witnessed recently.

Kerala red alert: Torrential rains lashing Kerala since August 1 have claimed 25 lives, left four people missing, and injured 10 others, the state government confirmed on Tuesday.The severe weather has completely destroyed 52 homes and partially damaged 565 properties, forcing over 18,000 displaced residents into more than 400 relief camps across the state.Pathanamthitta, Kottayam, and Alappuzha remain among the worst-affected districts, accounting for the vast majority of citizens currently seeking emergency shelter.
What has IMD said on Kerala rain?
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a red alert for eight districts—including Pathanamthitta, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur, and Kasaragod—warning of continued extremely heavy rainfall.Official weather data revealed that Kerala received nearly three times its normal rainfall during the four-day period, recording a 181 percent excess.With several low-lying and riverside areas inundated, rescue teams and local authorities remain on high alert to assist stranded residents.
Kerala received 205.8 mm of rainfall between August 1 and 4, against the normal 73.2 mm, recording an excess of 181 per cent, the data showed, as reported by PTI news agency.
Heavy rains continued to lash parts of Kerala
As heavy rains continued to lash parts of Kerala, the India Meteorological Department issued a ‘red alert’ for eight districts — Pathanamthitta, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod — on Tuesday.
IMD orange alert for these cities of Kerala
The IMD also issued an ‘orange alert’ in four districts — Alappuzha, Thrissur, Palakkad and Malappuram — and a ‘yellow alert’ in Thiruvananthapuram and Kollam districts. The weather agency issued an ‘orange alert’ in nine districts for Wednesday.
A ‘red alert’ indicates extremely heavy rainfall of over 20 cm in 24 hours, while an ‘orange alert’ signifies very heavy rainfall between 11 cm and 20 cm, and a ‘yellow alert’ indicates heavy rainfall between 6 cm and 11 cm.

articles.title: Brahmaputra Floods: Why Assam Needs a New Water Policy - Frontline Magazine
articles.full_text:
More than 1.3 lakh people have been affected, and over 87 have lost their lives in Assam’s floods this year, as of August 4. The reason the data this year is particularly important is that Assam recorded nearly a 30 per cent rainfall deficit until late July. And, even as 2026 was described globally as the heatwave year, suffering from the Godzilla El Niño, Assam still suffered from the devastation of flooding. This contradiction exposes an essential truth about Assam floods: floods in the State no longer occur simply because of the quantum of rainfall.
In Assam, the government’s focus usually revolves around embankments and relief camps, or on compensation to affected families after the floods. While these are undoubtedly essential responses, they do little to address the structural causes of flooding in the first place. When policies treat Assam as an isolated unit instead of seeing it as part of a shared river basin, they end up building structural measures that are of little help in protecting the Assam valley from the ravages of the mighty Brahmaputra.
The first failure is, thus, geographical. Most of the rivers passing through Assam generally originate in other regions like Tibet, or from States in northeastern India, such as Arunachal Pradesh. The rivers also receive flows from tributaries in Nagaland and Meghalaya before finally draining into Bangladesh. While water does not recognise State boundaries, flood governance in India largely operates along State lines. This fragmentation of water governance extends across a single river basin, such as, the Brahmaputra, a river that stretches across multiple States.
Since water is a State subject, flood measures are often scattered and diverse across State governments. A State-centric approach, therefore, cannot manage what is fundamentally a basin-wide problem, as the one faced in the Brahmaputra basin. This means the first priority when talking about managing or mitigating floods is that the focus has to shift from administrative thinking to river-basin governance. Hence, it becomes important to treat parts of northeastern India and parts of West Bengal as a single unit.
Second failure
The second failure lies in the institutional weakness of the Brahmaputra Board, which is the apex body that largely takes into account all areas under the Brahmaputra Basin. The board was established under the Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980, and it was then considered well suited to act as the nodal agency to prepare integrated master plans for flood control, erosion management, and drainage across the Brahmaputra basin.
The board has been reconstituted many times, most recently in 2019. Yet, despite this broad mandate, the board has remained largely an advisory institution with limited authority to ensure implementation. Its record reflects these limitations. Of the 73 master plans identified across the Brahmaputra, Barak, and other river basins, only 52 were approved until 2025, well short of the earlier targets that were set.
More than a decade ago, in 2010, a Comptroller and Auditor General report pointed to the absence of clear timelines, weak inter-agency coordination, and poor monitoring by the board. Even today, the implementation of plans depends largely on individual State governments, with no effective central mechanism to monitor compliance or execution. The board also continues to suffer from severe manpower shortages, as stated in a 2024 Lok Sabha reply by the Minister of State for Jal Shakti, Raj Bhushan Chawdhary, when 65 of the 182 sanctioned technical staff positions were vacant.
Third failure
The third failure is the Central and State governments' inability to replace this outdated institutional framework. In 2004, recognising the limitations of the Brahmaputra Board, the idea of a North-East Water Management Authority (NEWMA) was first proposed by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh. The plan resurfaced in 2022 when a draft Bill was listed in Parliament, proposing the repeal of the Brahmaputra Board Act and the creation of a single statutory authority for flood control, erosion management, water sharing, and integrated infrastructure planning across the northeastern region.
An authority such as NEWMA was envisioned to ensure that master plans are not merely prepared for the individual States but implemented by a single centralised authority through dedicated funding, clear timelines, and institutional accountability with the Central government undertaking the entire financial responsibility. Such a body could also facilitate coordination among the northeastern States while strengthening India’s ability to respond to emerging transboundary challenges, including upstream hydropower development on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, which is three times the world’s largest hydropower project and has the capacity to pose many challenges to water security in India. More importantly, a central body would finally align flood governance with the ecological reality of a shared river basin.
Finally, with climate change expected to make extreme rainfall events more frequent and the course of river systems more unpredictable, it is timely and important to shape infrastructure institutions in ways that they can help the most. If every flood season ends with relief packages, but begins with the same institutional weaknesses, the cycle of destruction will continue unabated.
India needs to envision the Brahmaputra as a single river basin, and reform the existing governance architecture. Reviving the proposal for NEWMA could be a first step in this reworking.
Abhay Tomar works as a research associate in the Office of the Chairperson, Parliamentary Standing Committee on Water Resources.
